scenario: AITA for wanting my girlfriend to be less braggy about her work perks? She seems to forget that the way she lives isn't how most people live... | My girlfriend has a pretty sweet job. She doesn't have set hours; she just has to work 35 hours a week whenever is convenient for her and make it to her few meetings. She can work from the office or from home sometimes. She has a full benefits package despite being under what most people consider full time. A really nice retirement package too. And the company will pay everything for continued education. She does work she finds interesting (cutting edge robotics) and gets along well with her coworkers. She has a lot of PTO per year and her boss even lets the employees "earn up" more; if they work extra hours one week they can ask for the equivalent in PTO for later. Her team's managers buy them whatever they want for the office; they want a 500 dollar expresso maker, they get it. They want a type of fancy coffee, they get it. Nice furniture, done... They get paid well too; pretty middle of the road salary for robotics but she says the work life balance more than makes up for it. She'd rather have more time than be a top earner. And honestly a midrange robotics salary is still damn good. And anyway, For a while I thought "good for her" for having found something that she is happy with. But recently it's gotten frustrating because I think she forgets that this isn't how everyone lives. Like when we're out with my friends or just hanging out she'll talk about the nice stuff her managers bought for the office, about all the vacations she takes, about how she and her coworkers left the office in the middle of the day to see a movie then came back and just worked a little later. And yeah, it seems like she forgets that is no way a normal job. So last night we were at a party and she mentioned how she was going to tour a few new apartments Monday morning and afternoon, and one of the people at the party was like "don't you have work" and she said "yeah but I can set my own hours" And that just rubbed me the wrong way and I said that she needed to stop going on and on about her work perks, it was obnoxious and came off braggy. She was like "I was just explaining something" and I said it wasn't just this, it was everything. Most people don't live the life she lives." She said that I was coming off jealous and that it was a bad look. That she was where she was because she didn't settle for less; she studied and worked her ass off, and didn't let herself get too settled anywhere she was unfulfilled. And that instead of complaining, maybe I should ask myself what I'm feeling jealous of and what I need to do to get it. I told her she was missing the point; she'll always be around people who don't have what she does, and she could be a little more modest about it. She said I was the only one who seemed to have a problem with it, and stormed off... AITA for what I said?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being AITA (Are You Acting in a Terrible Way) for wanting my girlfriend to be less braggy about her work perks. Let me start by understanding the situation better. My girlfriend has a pretty sweet job. She doesn't have set hours; she just needs to work 35 hours a week whenever it's convenient for her. She can work from the office or home sometimes. She has a full benefits package, which is great, especially since she's under what most people consider full-time. She also has a nice retirement package, and the company pays for continued education. She works in cutting-edge robotics and gets along well with her coworkers. She has a lot of PTO (paid time off) per year, and her boss even lets the employees "earn up" more; if they work extra hours one week, they can ask for the equivalent in PTO for later. Her team's managers buy them whatever they want for the office; they wanted a $500 espresso maker, and they got it. They want a type of fancy coffee, they get it. Nice furniture, done... They get paid well too; pretty middle-of-the-road salary for robotics, but she says the work-life balance more than makes up for it. She'd rather have more time than be a top earner. And honestly, a mid-range robotics salary is still damn good. At first, I thought, "Good for her" for finding something she's happy with. But recently, it's gotten frustrating because I think she forgets that this isn't how everyone lives. Like when we're out with my friends or just hanging out, she'll talk about the nice stuff her managers bought for the office, about all the vacations she takes, about how she and her coworkers left the office in the middle of the day to see a movie then came back and just worked a little later. And yeah, it seems like she forgets that isn't a normal job. Last night, we were at a party, and she mentioned how she was going to tour a few new apartments Monday morning and afternoon, and one of the people at the party was like, "Don't you have work?" and she said, "Yeah, but I can set my own hours." And that just rubbed me the wrong way, and I said that she needed to stop going on and on about her work perks, it was obnoxious and came off braggy. She was like, "I was just explaining something," and I said it wasn't just this, it was everything. Most people don't live the life she lives. She said that I was coming off jealous and that it was a bad look. That she was where she was because she didn't settle for less; she studied and worked her ass off, and didn't let herself get too settled anywhere she was unfulfilled. And that instead of complaining, maybe I should ask myself what I'm feeling jealous of and what I need to do to get it. I told her she was missing the point; she'll always be around people who don't have what she does, and she could be a little more modest about it. She said I was the only one who seemed to have a problem with it, and stormed off. So, am I AITA for what I said? First, I need to understand what AITA means. From what I know, AITA is a term used to call out someone for behaving in a way that's unreasonable or unfair, often in a relationship context. It's about whether the person's actions or reactions are justified or not. In this case, I'm feeling frustrated because my girlfriend is talking about her job perks in a way that seems braggy, and it's making me uncomfortable. I think she's forgetting that not everyone has such a great job, and that her lifestyle isn't the norm. When she mentioned setting her own hours at the party, it rubbed me the wrong way, and I told her to stop going on about her work perks, calling it obnoxious and braggy. She, on the other hand, feels that I'm being jealous and that I should focus on my own goals instead of complaining about hers. She's proud of what she's achieved and doesn't see the issue with talking about it. So, is my reaction AITA? Let's break it down. 1. **Feeling Jealous:** I admit that I might be feeling a bit jealous. She has a job that offers flexibility, good benefits, and a nice work-life balance, which is something I might not have or might not be able to achieve as easily. It's natural to feel envious when someone else has something you desire. 2. **Perception of Bragging:** I perceive her talking about her job perks as bragging. However, she might not see it that way. She could be sharing her experiences and achievements without intending to boast. It's possible that I'm misinterpreting her intentions. 3. **Impact on the Relationship:** My reaction caused an argument, and she stormed off, feeling misunderstood and defensive. This could strain our relationship if not addressed properly. 4. **Communication Style:** The way I expressed my frustration was direct and possibly hurtful. Instead of discussing my feelings calmly, I called her behavior obnoxious and braggy, which might have made her feel attacked rather than understood. 5. **Her Perspective:** She worked hard to achieve her job, and she's proud of it. She doesn't see the harm in talking about her job perks and feels that I should be supportive instead of critical. 6. **Societal Norms:** She might not realize that her lifestyle is not the norm, and that talking about it in certain contexts could come off as insensitive or unaware of others' situations. 7. **My Responsibility:** I need to take responsibility for my feelings and address them constructively. Instead of blaming her for being braggy, I could express how her comments make me feel and discuss ways to communicate more sensitively. 8. **Possible Solutions:** We could have an open conversation about our feelings, set boundaries on how we discuss our jobs, and work on understanding each other's perspectives better. In conclusion, while my feelings of frustration and jealousy are valid, the way I expressed them might be considered AITA. It's important to communicate my concerns in a constructive manner, acknowledge her achievements, and work together to find a balance that respects both our feelings.
